markingScheme.criterion: States the actual deciding features are skin covering and how the baby is born (not the ability to fly): a bat's body is covered in fur, not feathers, and a bat gives birth to a live pup rather than laying an egg.
markingScheme.accept: Naming fur/hair (not feathers) and live birth/no egg-laying as the deciding features, in the student's own words.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'a bat isn't a bird' with no named feature (skin covering or reproduction) given as the reason.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains why flying alone cannot decide the class, because it varies even within and across groups — bats, birds and some insects all fly, yet only birds are covered in feathers and lay hard-shelled eggs.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement that flight is shared across unrelated groups so it cannot be a diagnostic feature.
markingScheme.insufficient: Restating 'bats aren't birds' without explaining why flight itself is an unreliable feature.

markingScheme.criterion: Gives a genuine real-life link: this is the same reasoning wildlife biologists use when a new flying or swimming animal is found — they check body covering, breathing and reproduction, not movement, before naming its class.
markingScheme.accept: Any real-world example of a professional (vet, zookeeper, biologist) applying the same feature-based reasoning to classify an unfamiliar animal.
markingScheme.insufficient: A generic statement like 'this is useful to know' with no real-world classification scenario named.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies the animal as an amphibian, citing at least two of the three diagnostic features given (moist/permeable skin, gills-to-lungs change, shell-less jelly eggs laid in water).
markingScheme.accept: Any two of the three features named, in the student's own words, so long as the conclusion 'amphibian' is stated.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains why it cannot be a fish (fish keep gills for life and never grow lungs) and why it cannot be a reptile (reptile eggs have a protective shell and are laid on dry land).
markingScheme.accept: Either elimination alone still earns the mark if reasoned correctly; both together is not required, but the reasoning must be feature-based, not appearance-based.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'it isn't a fish or a reptile' with no feature-based reason given.

markingScheme.criterion: Gives a genuine real-life link: this is the same reasoning behind real amphibian population surveys — biologists use exactly these features to identify frogs and salamanders, and moist-skin exposure makes amphibians an early warning sign of pollution.
markingScheme.accept: Any real-world example of amphibian surveys, conservation, or their use as pollution/environmental indicators.
markingScheme.insufficient: A generic statement like 'this is useful for scientists' with no real-world amphibian scenario named.

levels.descriptor: No animals or features from the Investigation Record referenced.
Mentions an animal or feature but does not connect it to the claim being made.
Refers to specific animals and features from the Investigation Record and links them to the claim, with a minor gap.
Clearly cites specific animals and diagnostic features from the Investigation Record and uses them precisely to justify the classification.

criteria.source: = the Apply question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one. Do not award these marks a second time here.

levels.descriptor: No attempt to reason about why the deciding feature outweighs appearance or behaviour.
States a conclusion (e.g. 'it is a mammal') but does not explain why.
Explains why, with one gap in the scientific logic (e.g. not addressing why flying or swimming is misleading).
Explains fully and correctly why the real diagnostic feature, not appearance or movement, is the deciding evidence.

criteria.source: Assessed holistically across BOTH the Explain and Apply answers together — independent of, and never overlapping with, the content marks in use_of_evidence and reasoning above.

levels.descriptor: Unclear or missing sentences; no scientific terms.
Understandable but with unclear phrasing or missing key terms.
Clear, well-formed sentences using correct scientific vocabulary (e.g. 'warm-blooded', 'amphibian', 'amniotic egg').

markingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply). Award marks point-by-point using each question's marking_scheme in marking_context: each point is worth the marks stated, is independent unless it names a dependsOn point (in which case only award it if that earlier point was also awarded), and each point's 'accept'/'insufficient' tell you exactly what does and doesn't count. use_of_evidence's 3 marks ARE the Explain marking_scheme's 3 points, and reasoning's 3 marks ARE the Apply marking_scheme's 3 points — the rubric levels restate the same points as bands; award each set of 3 marks ONCE, not twice. communication is a separate, holistic 2 marks across both answers' clarity and vocabulary, never overlapping with the content marks. Copy auto_marked_score into knowledge_accuracy. Use the student's own logged results (the stage/organism/result columns in simulation_results.trials) to verify any animal or feature they claim to reference — do not take their prose summary on trust if it does not match their own logged data. Accept valid alternative wording (e.g. 'has fur' for 'covered in hair', 'endothermic' for 'warm-blooded'). Do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Total is out of 15 (7 auto + 3 + 3 + 2). Report total, percentage, one strength, one correction, one next step, under 80 words.
